stories.headline: Broncos fall to Chiefs 31-10 in Monday Night Football season opener at Arrowhead
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos dropped their 2026 season opener Monday night, losing 31-10 to the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium in a game that aired on Monday Night Football. Quarterback Bo Nix connected with tight end Evan Engram for Denver's lone touchdown, but the offense struggled to generate consistent production against Kansas City's defense.

The lopsided loss exposed areas the Broncos coaching staff will need to address heading into Week 2. Denver gave up the most missed tackle yards in Next Gen Stats history during the game, according to postgame reports, a stark indicator of the team's defensive breakdowns.

Fans had gathered at McGregor Square in downtown Denver to watch the opener, marking the return of Monday Night Football to the Broncos' schedule. Head coach Sean Payton acknowledged the team has corrections to make as it prepares for its next contest.

stories.headline: Joe Sakic steps back into Avalanche GM role; no search planned, sources say
stories.summary:
The Colorado Avalanche will not conduct a general manager search following the departure of Chris MacFarland, who left for Nashville, as team president Joe Sakic has agreed to take on the full-time GM role, multiple team sources confirmed to the Denver Gazette. Sakic previously served as GM before stepping down in 2022 after leading Colorado to a Stanley Cup championship.

Sources describe Sakic as "reinvigorated" since accepting the position in June, with the Avalanche's sweep at the hands of the Vegas Golden Knights in the Western Conference Final reportedly fueling his competitive drive. The team is satisfied with its supporting front-office staff, including assistant GMs Kevin McDonald and Andrew Wilson and special assistant Andrew Cogliano.

The expectation is that Sakic will handle the GM duties full-time for the 2026-27 season, with the organization reassessing the arrangement beyond that. Colorado's training camp opens Thursday.

stories.headline: Aaron Gordon opens up on Peyton Watson trade: 'Deeper than basketball'
stories.summary:
Denver Nuggets forward Aaron Gordon spoke candidly Sunday about the offseason sign-and-trade that sent Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers in exchange for two draft picks, calling Watson "like my brother" and saying their bond extends beyond the court. Gordon made the remarks before hosting a FlexWork Sports youth basketball camp in Lakewood.

Watson signed a four-year, $88 million contract with Cleveland after tense negotiations with Denver, which held his rights as a restricted free agent. Gordon and Watson had vacationed together earlier this summer, celebrating former teammate Michael Porter Jr.'s birthday in France, and the two families attend the same church.

Gordon, who turns 31 Wednesday, said he has spent much of his summer training in Denver and organizing team activities, including a bonding trip to Puerto Rico where the squad used a facility built by Nuggets assistant coach JJ Barea. Jokic, Murray and Christian Braun were unable to attend, but most of the roster participated.

stories.headline: Supreme Court preserves Colorado mail voting ahead of November midterms
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled Monday that states must continue sending mail ballots under existing processes, blocking a Trump administration plan that would have required uniform envelope styles and mandated the U.S. Postal Service to cross-check voter lists before delivering ballots. The ruling came with roughly 50 days remaining before the November 3 midterms.

Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, the Democratic nominee for state attorney general, applauded the decision, saying Trump's effort to restrict who could receive a mail ballot "has failed." Colorado relies heavily on mail voting, which Griswold has called the state's "gold standard" election system.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented, while Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed the restrictions should not apply to the upcoming midterms but left open the possibility of ruling for the administration in a future case. Several states had already begun mailing ballots to voters before the ruling was issued.

stories.headline: Six Aurora teens to face charges following August 'teen takeover' near Del Mar Park
stories.summary:
Aurora police announced Monday that six boys identified as participants in the August 30 "teen takeover" near Del Mar Park will face criminal charges including assault, reckless endangerment, disorderly conduct, theft and injury to property. Two teens have already been arrested, while arrest warrants have been submitted for four others; all six are boys between the ages of 13 and 17.

The incident unfolded after an estimated 750 to 1,000 people, most of them teenagers, gathered in the Hoffman Heights shopping center parking lot near East Sixth Avenue and Peoria Street following an unpermitted basketball event. The crowd rapidly became unruly, with attendees vandalizing property, stealing from nearby businesses including a restaurant and a grocery store, and committing assaults — one of which left a person unconscious at Del Mar Park.

Aurora Police Chief Todd Chamberlain said dozens of officers were rerouted from across the city to disperse the crowd. Additional arrests are possible as investigators continue identifying individuals who damaged property or committed other crimes. The incident follows similar teen gatherings that disrupted businesses at The Shops at Northfield in June.

stories.headline: Two teens killed in wrong-way crash on I-70 near Rifle
stories.summary:
Two people died early Sunday morning in a wrong-way, head-on collision involving two passenger vehicles and a semitrailer on westbound Interstate 70 near Rifle, the Colorado State Patrol reported. Troopers responded to the crash at mile marker 93 at approximately 2:30 a.m.

A 17-year-old boy driving a 2022 Subaru eastbound in the westbound lanes struck a 2004 GMC Yukon head-on, according to investigators. The GMC driver, an 18-year-old woman, then collided with a Peterbilt semitrailer in the adjacent lane. Both the Subaru and GMC drivers were pronounced dead at the scene; the semitrailer driver was uninjured.

Neither victim had been publicly identified as of Monday, pending notification by the Garfield County Coroner's Office. The crash remained under investigation by the Colorado State Patrol.

stories.headline: Denver's Milpero earns Michelin star; 15 Colorado restaurants newly recognized in 2026
stories.summary:
Denver's Milpero, a Mexican tasting-menu restaurant in the River North neighborhood, was awarded a Michelin star Monday, becoming the 10th starred restaurant in Colorado. Chef Johnny Curiel, who also holds stars for Alma Fonda Fina and Mezcaleria Alma, now has three Michelin-recognized restaurants in Denver.

The 2026 Michelin Guide recognized 15 Colorado restaurants in total this year, bringing the statewide count of recognized establishments to 63. The expanded recognition comes after the guide's three-year exclusive contract — which limited coverage to Denver, Boulder, Aspen and Snowmass Village, and Vail and Beaver Creek — expired and was replaced by a broader statewide agreement backed by a $100,000 annual commitment from the Colorado Tourism Office.

New Bib Gourmand recipients include Annette in Aurora, Pig and Tiger and Rougarou in Denver. Eleven additional restaurants across Aurora, Breckenridge, Colorado Springs and Telluride were added to the guide's recommended list. All nine previously starred Colorado restaurants retained their designations.

stories.headline: Aspen Snowmass offering $3.75 lift tickets for 80th anniversary celebration in December
stories.summary:
Aspen Snowmass is selling a limited number of lift tickets for $3.75 to mark the ski company's 80th anniversary, valid for December 14 — the date the resort was founded in 1946. The company is also offering $80 tickets for December 12 and 13, all valid across Aspen Mountain, Aspen Highlands, Buttermilk and Snowmass.

Typical single-day lift tickets at Aspen Snowmass range from $189 to $309 depending on the time of season, making the anniversary pricing a significant discount that the resort expects to sell out quickly. The promotion mirrors the price reportedly charged when the resort first opened under founders Friedl Pfeifer and Walter Paepcke.

Additional anniversary festivities will include on-mountain après parties and $19.46 food and beverage specials at on-mountain restaurants — a nod to the founding year. Discounted tickets are available through the resort's website under the 80th anniversary section.

stories.headline: New racket sports club set to open in Broomfield; Soda Club brings Michelin-recognized vegan pasta to RiNo
stories.summary:
The Three Rackets, a 34,000-square-foot facility combining pickleball, padel and squash under one roof, is preparing to open at 830 Hoyt St. in Broomfield with a soft opening scheduled for September 21. The club was founded by former professional squash players and brothers Mark and Chris Fuller along with Chris Douglass, and will offer coaching, leagues, social spaces and dining.

Memberships start at $87.50 per month for single-sport access and $125 for full access. Court fees begin at $20 for squash, $30 for pickleball and $60 for padel, with reduced off-peak player rates available.

Also opening this month in Denver's River North Arts District, Soda Club — a Michelin Bib Gourmand winner from New York City's East Village — has launched at The Ramble Hotel at 1260 25th St. The restaurant, run by Colorado-native restaurateur Ravi Derossi, serves fresh vegan pasta dishes and natural wines with a Mediterranean influence and can seat up to 100 guests indoors and outdoors.

stories.headline: Fall weather arrives in Denver this week; Thursday brings best chance for metro rain
stories.summary:
A cold front moving through Colorado late Monday night will bring noticeably cooler temperatures to the Denver metro area Tuesday, with highs expected only in the low to mid-70s, down from the 90s recorded over the weekend. Breezy northerly winds and lows in the low 50s are forecast for Tuesday morning.

Moisture levels will remain unusually high for mid-September, but cooler air should limit storm development across the plains, with the mountains seeing the better chance for showers and thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon. Temperatures will rebound slightly to the low 80s by Wednesday before another round of moisture arrives.

Thursday is forecast as the best opportunity for meaningful rainfall in the Denver metro area, as an upper-level low pushes monsoonal moisture into Colorado and could produce locally heavy rain in some areas. A general chance for afternoon storms is expected to persist through the weekend, particularly in the mountains, with highs staying in the upper 70s to low 80s into early next week.

stories.headline: Longmont regenerative rancher grows million-dollar beef business amid Trump import plan disruption
stories.summary:
Andy Breiter, founder of Grama Grass & Livestock in Longmont, has built a million-dollar regenerative beef operation by rotating cattle across 700 acres of public and private land in Boulder County, growing from 25 cows on one pasture in 2020 to an average herd of 90 cows across 20 pastures and 85,000 pounds of beef sold in 2025. His model relies on partnerships with the city of Boulder's Open Space and Mountain Parks Department, the city of Louisville and private landowners.

Breiter's success comes as the broader U.S. cattle industry faces significant disruption from Trump administration trade policies, including an August 21 announcement that 300,000 metric tons of foreign lean beef trimmings would be imported and blended into American ground beef at roughly 25 percent below current market prices. Travis Grant, CEO of the Colorado Livestock Association, said the imported product has less fat than domestically raised beef.

Breiter's direct-to-consumer and local restaurant model has helped insulate him from the price volatility affecting larger operations. His beef is sold at locations including Denver's Coperta restaurant, Lucky's Market in Boulder and the Organic Sandwich Company in Louisville.

stories.headline: Colorado ranchers join CSU researchers to track fertilizer runoff in Yampa, Gunnison river basins
stories.summary:
Farmers and ranchers in Colorado's Yampa and Gunnison river basins are partnering with Colorado State University and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment to monitor agricultural water quality as rising stream temperatures and shrinking flows linked to climate change trigger algae blooms in some of the state's most pristine waterways. The effort uses best management practices rather than strict regulations, an approach that has helped attract rancher participation.

Philip Rossi, who farms hay and runs a cattle operation in the Upper Yampa River Basin above Stagecoach Reservoir, was among the first to allow scientists to monitor irrigation runoff from his fields. Initial results found little fertilizer reaching nearby streams, and the use of unfertilized grass buffer strips has reduced that number further.

With the first three-year study complete, a broader follow-up effort is underway that will add stream temperature monitoring across additional ranches. Erik Wardle, director of CSU's Agricultural Water Quality Program, said early skepticism among ranchers has largely given way to enthusiasm, with about 85 percent of current participation now driven by producers themselves. Toxic algae blooms have already been documented in Stagecoach Reservoir and Steamboat Lake.

topStory.headline: Supreme Court Blocks Trump Administration Mail Ballot Rule Ahead of Midterms
topStory.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected an emergency application from the Trump administration seeking to reinstate a new U.S. Postal Service regulation governing mail-in ballots, leaving a lower court ruling blocking the rule in place. The court appeared divided 7-2, with Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissenting. The decision prevents the regulation from taking effect before the 2026 midterm elections.

The blocked rule would have required states to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service, which would then verify that ballots were sent only to individuals on those lists before delivering them. States would also have been required to follow Postal Service directives on ballot envelope design. Challengers argued the rule represented an extraordinary expansion of federal executive authority over state-administered elections and would have caused widespread disruption with balloting already underway in some states, including North Carolina, which began sending ballots on Sept. 4.

The legal challenge was led by California and a coalition of states alongside nonprofit groups including the League of Women Voters and the Campaign Legal Center. California Attorney General Rob Bonta called the decision 'a victory for our democracy and a powerful affirmation of the rule of law.' Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund, said the ruling made clear that 'the Constitution does not give the president unilateral authority governing federal elections regarding mail voting.' Justice Alito, in dissent, said the federal government had the stronger legal argument, though he acknowledged that concerns about implementation logistics gave him pause.

The rule originated from an executive order President Trump signed in March directing the Postal Service to take a role in verifying ballot distribution. Trump has repeatedly and without evidence characterized mail-in voting as susceptible to widespread fraud. A whistleblower within the Postal Service had reportedly warned of significant operational risks in attempting to screen mail-in ballots at scale. Trevor Potter, president of the Campaign Legal Center, said he remained confident the underlying executive order would ultimately be found unconstitutional and permanently blocked.

The ruling carries significant implications for election administration across all 50 states heading into the midterm cycle. Election officials and voting rights advocates said implementing the rule on short notice would have created confusion for voters and jeopardized local officials' ability to administer elections. The decision reinforces longstanding precedent that states hold primary authority over election administration, a principle cited by several parties to the case, including Travis County, Texas Clerk Dyana Limon-Mercado and the Arizona Students' Association.
